js(m, z) = √(π/(2z))·besselj(m + ½, z), which equals SpecialFunctions.sphericalbesselj. At z = 0 it returns the limit (1 for order 0, 0 otherwise). For an integer order and a real argument the result is real.
ys(m, z) = √(π/(2z))·bessely(m + ½, z), as SpecialFunctions.sphericalbessely; z must be non-zero.

Γ(z) is gamma(z), also for complex z. At a pole (0, −1, …) or on overflow (Γ(172)) the result is an error instead of Julia's Inf or NaN. Γ(a, x) is the upper incomplete gamma function ∫ₓ^∞ t^(a−1)e^(−t) dt, computed as gamma(a, x) in extended precision; it needs a > 0 and x ≥ 0. Type it with G Ctrl+G.
Where Γ is negative the result is complex (the principal logarithm), as loggamma of a complex number; Julia's logabsgamma would return the logarithm of the absolute value instead.
Psi(y) is digamma(y); Psi(n, y) is polygamma(n, y), the n-th derivative, with n a non-negative integer.
The Gauss hypergeometric function 2F1(a, b; c; x), for real arguments with −1 < x < 1 only (Julia's function also continues outside). Returns 1 when a, b or x is 0.
The confluent hypergeometric function <sub>1</sub>F<sub>1</sub>(a; b; x) for real arguments.
ibeta(a, x, y) is the regularised incomplete beta function Ia(x, y), the first value of beta_inc(x, y, a). Note the order: the integration limit comes first. It needs 0 ≤ a ≤ 1 and x, y > 0.
The Jacobi polynomial Pn(a, b)(x) by its three-term recurrence; a, b > −1, n a non-negative integer. Element by element on x. Julia's standard library has no Jacobi polynomial.
Scaled: J0(z)·e^(−|Im z|). Type the name with a literal subscript, J0.sc.

Heaviside step. Φ(0) = 0.5, where some definitions use 0 or 1.
The Levi-Civita symbol of rank 3: +1 for an even permutation of the indices, −1 for an odd one, 0 when two are equal. The indices run from ORIGIN to ORIGIN + 2.

1/sin(z); a zero sine is the error "can't divide by zero" instead of Inf. Of a square matrix it is the matrix function (as Julia's method for matrices); of any other array it applies element by element.

sin(z)/z with the value 1 at 0. This is the unnormalised sinc; Julia's sinc(x) is sin(πx)/(πx). Element by element on arrays.
asin(1/z), complex where the real value does not exist. Of a square matrix it is the matrix function (as Julia's method for matrices); of any other array it applies element by element.

atanh(1/z), complex where needed. Of a square matrix it is the matrix function (as Julia's method for matrices); of any other array it applies element by element.

A negative real number gives the complex root (sqrt(−4) = 2i), where Julia's real method throws. Units are kept: sqrt(9 m²) = 3 m. Of a square matrix it is the matrix function (as Julia's method for matrices); of any other array it applies element by element. Same as the root operator.

A result larger than about 10^307 is an error instead of Inf. The argument must be dimensionless. Of a square matrix it is the matrix function (as Julia's method for matrices); of any other array it applies element by element.

The natural logarithm. A negative real argument gives the principal complex value (ln(−1) = πi), where Julia's real method throws; ln(0) is an error instead of −Inf. Of a square matrix it is the matrix function (as Julia's method for matrices); of any other array it applies element by element.

log(z) is the base-10 logarithm (Julia's log10), not the natural logarithm as Julia's log(z). log(z, b) is the logarithm in base b, computed as ln(z)/ln(b); note that Julia's log(b, z) takes the base first.
As ln, but returns −10^307 at 0 instead of an error, which keeps plots and sums of logarithmic data finite.
Element by element; a complex number is rounded part by part. Units are kept.
As floor.
As floor: rounds towards zero.

round(z, n) rounds to n decimals (default 0; negative n rounds to tens, hundreds…). Halves round away from zero (round(2.5) = 3), whereas Julia's default rounds halves to even (round(2.5) = 2.0); this is Julia's RoundNearestTiesAway.
floor(z/y)·y: the greatest multiple of y not above z. Useful with units: Floor(1.234 m, 5 cm) = 1.2 m.
ceil(z/y)·y.
round(z/y)·y with halves away from zero.
trunc(z/y)·y.
atan2(x, y) is Julia's atan(y, x): note that x comes first here and second in Julia. The result is in (−π, π]; both arguments need the same unit; (0, 0) is an error.
Element by element.
Element by element.
Absolute value or complex modulus, element by element on arrays. The operator |x| differs on arrays: it gives the length of a vector and the determinant of a square matrix.
−1, 0 or 1 for a real number; units are ignored. Complex numbers are an error (use signum).
z/|z|, also for complex z (as Julia's sign of a complex number); at 0 it returns the optional second argument, 1 by default, where Julia returns 0.
1 when z is in the right half-plane or on the positive imaginary axis, −1 otherwise, 0 at 0.
The principal argument in (−π, π], as Julia's angle; arg(0) = 0. Units are ignored.
The angle of the point (x, y) in [0, 2π), measured counter-clockwise from the positive x axis; Julia's atan(y, x) plus 2π when negative. (0, 0) is an error.
1 for a number or a quantity, real or complex; 0 for arrays, strings and functions. Julia equivalent: x isa Number.
1 for a vector or matrix. Julia equivalent: x isa AbstractArray.
1 when the argument is a function (a built-in, your own or a Julia function). Julia equivalent: x isa Function.
1 when the argument is a range variable.

One unit of the argument's dimension in SI base units: SIUnitsOf(3 km) = 1 m; 1 for a dimensionless number. Divide by it to strip the unit: x/SIUnitsOf(x). Similar to oneunit(upreferred(x)) in Unitful.
1 for a string. Julia equivalent: x isa AbstractString.
Element by element; 1 when the real or the imaginary part is NaN; 0 for strings and other values that are not numbers (Julia's isnan throws for them).

if(c, a, b) returns a when c is non-zero and b otherwise. Unlike Julia's ifelse, which evaluates both arguments, only the chosen branch is evaluated (like Julia's ternary c ? a : b), so the other branch may contain an expression that would fail.
Raises an error with the given message, shown on the region; a try in a program catches it.
Joins two or more strings; every argument must be a string (use num2str for numbers). Julia's string or * also converts other values.
The number of characters (Unicode code points), not bytes; Julia's sizeof counts bytes.

substr(S, m, n): n characters starting at position m. Positions count from ORIGIN like array indices (0 by default), whereas Julia string indices are 1-based byte indices. A count past the end stops at the end.
search(S, T, m): the position of the first T in S at or after position m, counted from ORIGIN, or −1 when it is absent (Julia's findnext returns nothing and a 1-based range).
The number as text with at most three decimals, trailing zeros dropped; complex numbers as a+bi; quantities with their unit. Julia's string writes the full precision.
Reads a real or complex constant: "1.5", "-2e3", "1+2i", "3j". Anything else is an error. Julia's parse(Float64, s) reads real numbers only.
A string from a vector of character codes; only 9, 10, 13 and 32 to 255 are accepted.
A column vector of the Unicode code points of the characters.
format("Span {0} m, load {1}", L, q) replaces {0}, {1}, … with the arguments, numbers formatted as by num2str. Placeholders count from 0 regardless of ORIGIN.

The remainder of x/y with the sign of x (truncated division), which is Julia's rem, not Julia's mod (which takes the sign of y): mod(−7, 3) = −1. Units must agree; y must not be zero. Element by element.
The binomial coefficient, computed exactly with big integers and returned as a double. Needs integers with n ≥ k ≥ 0.
The number of ordered selections of k out of n, n!/(n − k)!.
Of any number of integers or integer arrays; dimensionless only; the result is non-negative.
As gcd.
Places arrays top to bottom; a scalar counts as a 1 × 1 block. All arguments need the same number of columns. Elements may be of mixed kinds (numbers, strings, arrays).
Places arrays side by side; a scalar counts as a 1 × 1 block. All arguments need the same number of rows.

submatrix(A, ir, jr, ic, jc) is Julia's A[ir:jr, ic:jc] with indices counted from ORIGIN. Reversed bounds (jr < ir) return the rows or columns in reverse order. The result is always a matrix, also when it is 1 × 1.
An n × n identity matrix of doubles, as Matrix(1.0I, n, n).
matrix(m, n, f) builds an m × n matrix with element (i, j) equal to f(i, j), where i and j count from 0 whatever ORIGIN is. Julia equivalent: [f(i, j) for i in 0:m-1, j in 0:n-1].
A vector gives the square diagonal matrix (diagm); a square matrix gives the column of its diagonal (diag). Julia's diag also accepts non-square matrices.

npts points spaced evenly on a logarithmic scale from min to max, both included; both must be positive and have the same unit, which the points keep. Julia equivalent: exp10.(range(log10(a), log10(b), length=n)).
dec·dnpts points 10^(minexp + k/dnpts), k = 0, 1, …: whole decades starting at 10minexp, without the start of the next decade.

vec(x, y, z) is the column from x to z with step y − x, vec(x, z) with step 1 (−1 when z < x), and vec(i) turns a range variable into a vector. Unlike Julia's vec, which reshapes an array into a vector, this function builds a vector from a range, as collect(x:step:z).

The Jacobian matrix of a column-vector expression F(x) with respect to the column vector x, by numeric differentiation (Richardson extrapolation of central differences, the method of derivative). The optional k uses only the first k variables.
size(A, 1); 0 when the argument is not an array.
size(A, 2); 0 when the argument is not an array.
The number of elements of a column vector. A matrix or a row vector is an error (Julia's length counts every element).
The index of the last element of a vector: length(v) − 1 + ORIGIN. Julia's lastindex is always the length because Julia counts from 1.
The sum of the diagonal of a square matrix; the elements may carry units.
The numerical rank from the singular values, with Julia's default tolerance. The matrix must be numeric and without units.

The eigenvalues as a column vector, in Julia's order: ascending and real for a symmetric or Hermitian matrix (computed with Hermitian), otherwise sorted by real part, then imaginary part. A complex result whose imaginary parts are all zero is returned as real.

The normalised eigenvectors as columns, in the order of eigenvals, with the signs LAPACK chooses. eigenvecs(M, "L") returns left eigenvectors, which Julia does not compute directly (they are the right eigenvectors of the adjoint, paired by eigenvalue).

The largest element over all arguments, scalars and arrays together. Strings are compared alphabetically. For complex values it returns the largest real part plus i times the largest imaginary part, which Julia does not define. Units must agree.
As max, the smallest.
opnorm(M, 1): the largest absolute column sum. Note that Julia's norm(M, 1) is the sum of all absolute values, a different number.
opnorm(M, 2): the largest singular value.
norm(M): the Frobenius (Euclidean) norm.
opnorm(M, Inf): the largest absolute row sum.
‖M‖₁·‖M⁻¹‖₁ with operator norms, as cond(M, 1); Inf for a singular matrix.
The ratio of the largest to the smallest singular value, as cond(M).
norm(M)·norm(inv(M)) with the Frobenius norm. Julia's cond has no Frobenius variant.
As cond(M, Inf).
The Moore–Penrose pseudo-inverse; for a matrix of full column rank it is the least-squares left inverse.

Solves M·x = v: with LU decomposition for a square non-singular matrix (Julia's M \ v), and with the pseudo-inverse (least squares) for a non-square matrix. A singular square matrix is an error. v may have several columns.
The generalised eigenvalues of M·x = λ·N·x, as eigvals(M, N), in Julia's order.
The generalised eigenvectors, normalised to length 1, in the order of genvals. "L" as third argument returns left eigenvectors.
One unit eigenvector for the eigenvalue z, by inverse iteration on M − z·I. z need only be close to an eigenvalue. Julia has no single-eigenvector function; take the matching column of eigvecs.
The Kronecker product.
The reduced row echelon form, by Gauss–Jordan elimination with partial pivoting; entries below a tolerance proportional to the machine precision count as zero. Julia's standard library has no rref.
The sum of all elements, row by row, keeping units; an empty array sums to 0. The same as the operator Σv.
The matrix augment(Q, R) with the full m × m orthogonal Q and the m × n upper triangular R from Julia's Householder QR. Kept for older worksheets; prefer QR.
The lower triangular L with M = L·Lᴴ, as cholesky(Hermitian(M)).L. Kept for older worksheets; prefer Cholesky.

A nested vector [P; L]: by default with pivoting (RowMaximum), so that P·M·Pᵀ = L·Lᴴ. Cholesky(M, 0) turns pivoting off (P is the identity); a non-zero third argument returns the upper factor Lᴴ. Extract the parts with an index: Cholesky(M)[1].
A nested vector [P; L; U] with P·M = L·U (partial pivoting). Julia returns a factorisation object with a permutation vector instead of the matrix P.
A nested vector [P; Q; R] with M·P = Q·R, columns pivoted by decreasing norm (ColumnNorm); QR(M, 0) returns [Q; R] with M = Q·R. Q is the full square factor. Signs are LAPACK's.
The singular values in descending order, as a column.
A nested vector [U; S; V] with the thin factors in Julia's order, A = U·diag(S)·Vᵀ. Unpack it with [U; S; V] := svd(A); [U; S; Wᵀ] := svd(A) defines W as Vᵀ.

The indices of the elements of A equal to z, counted from ORIGIN. For a matrix each match is a vector [row; column], scanned column by column. An optional modifier selects otherwise: "eq", "not", "gt", "lt", "geq", "leq", "near" (closest values) or "range" (the interval of an ascending vector that holds z), or a function f(element, z). No match is an error (so a try can catch it). Julia equivalent: findall, whose indices start at 1.
Ascending by real part; a row or column vector keeps its orientation; a matrix is an error. The imaginary part is ignored.
Reverses a vector, or the order of the rows of a matrix (Julia's reverse(A, dims=1)).
Rows rearranged so that column n (counted from ORIGIN) ascends; stable. Julia equivalent: sortslices(A, dims=1, by=r -> r[n]).
Columns rearranged so that row n ascends; stable.
The elements of B at the positions where A matches z (with the modifiers of match), as a column in column-wise order. A and B must have the same size.
Searches the first column of A for z and returns column c (counted from ORIGIN) of the matching rows.
Searches the first row of A and returns row r of the matching columns, as a column vector.
The element at the first row whose first entry matches z1 and the first column whose first entry matches z2.
The rank of each element (1 for the smallest); tied elements get the mean of their ranks. Not to be confused with rank, the matrix rank.
The indices, counted from ORIGIN, that put v in ascending order; stable. Julia's sortperm returns 1-based indices.
The same function as convolve, under an older name.

Convolution of a signal with a kernel. For two vectors the full result has n + m − 1 elements; for matrices the result has the size of the signal. BC chooses the boundary (0 zero padding, the default; 1 circular; 2 reflect; 3 continue) and OV the initial overlap of the kernel (1 in 1-D, the centred kernel in 2-D by default). Computed directly in the time domain. The operator A ∗ B is the linear convolution and A ⊛ B the circular one.
The cross-correlation: the convolution with the kernel reversed (rotated by 180° for matrices), with the same boundary and overlap options as convolve.

The first n − m + 1 elements of the circular deconvolution of vz (n elements) by vx (m elements), computed with FFTs; an exact quotient comes back as polynomial division gives it, otherwise the minimum-norm circular solution.
The arithmetic mean over every element of every argument, scalars and arrays together (Julia's mean takes one collection). Units are kept and must agree.
Over every element of every argument; real values only; the mean of the two middle values for an even count.
The population variance, dividing by N, which is Julia's var(x, corrected=false); Julia's default var divides by N − 1 (that is Var here). Complex values use |x − mean|².
The sample variance, dividing by N − 1: Julia's default var.
The population standard deviation (divides by N), Julia's std(x, corrected=false). Julia's default std corresponds to Stdev.
The sample standard deviation (divides by N − 1), Julia's default std.
The geometric mean of positive numbers without units, (∏xᵢ)^(1/n), computed through logarithms when the product would overflow.
The harmonic mean n/Σ(1/xᵢ) of positive numbers; units are kept.
The most frequent value; when several values are equally frequent, the smallest. Real values only.
The value below which the fraction p (0 to 1) of the data lies, interpolating linearly between order statistics at position p·(n − 1). This matches Julia's default quantile(v, p).
Σ(aᵢ − ā)·conj(bᵢ − b̄)/N: the population covariance, dividing by N, over all elements of two arrays of equal size. Julia's cov divides by N − 1 unless corrected=false.
The same formula as cvar, for two vectors.
Pearson's correlation coefficient cvar(A, B)/(stdev(A)·stdev(B)); the same value as Julia's cor.
The vector [F; p]: the ratio of the two sample variances and the two-sided probability from the F distribution with (n₁ − 1, n₂ − 1) degrees of freedom.

Spearman's rank correlation as a vector of five values: the sum of squared rank differences D, its normal score and two-sided probability, ρ, and the probability of ρ from Student's t distribution. Ties get average ranks.
Kendall's τb, its z-score from the normal approximation with the tie correction of the variance, and the two-sided probability, as SciPy's kendalltau.
Kendall's τ<sub>b</sub> from a contingency table of frequencies, with its z-score and two-sided probability (without tie correction of the variance).
For a contingency table: Pearson's χ², the degrees of freedom, the upper-tail probability, Cramér's V and the contingency coefficient C.

The sample skewness n/((n−1)(n−2))·Σz³ with z standardised by the sample standard deviation (the adjusted Fisher–Pearson coefficient, as spreadsheets compute it). Julia's StatsBase.skewness returns the unadjusted value.
The excess sample kurtosis with the small-sample correction used by spreadsheets. StatsBase.kurtosis returns the unadjusted excess kurtosis.
pdf(Beta(s1, s2), x). Shape parameters s1, s2 > 0, as Julia's Beta(α, β). All arguments are dimensionless real numbers; x may be an array (element by element).
cdf(Beta(s1, s2), x), the probability of a value up to x. Shape parameters s1, s2 > 0, as Julia's Beta(α, β).
quantile(Beta(s1, s2), p), the inverse of pbeta; p between 0 and 1. Shape parameters s1, s2 > 0, as Julia's Beta(α, β).
A column of m random numbers, rand(rng, Beta(s1, s2), m), drawn from Equavela's shared random generator (see Seed). Shape parameters s1, s2 > 0, as Julia's Beta(α, β).

pdf(Binomial(n, q), x). n trials with success probability q, evaluated at k successes. For a non-integer argument the probability is 0. All arguments are dimensionless real numbers; x may be an array (element by element).
cdf(Binomial(n, q), x), the probability of a value up to x. The argument is rounded down to an integer first. n trials with success probability q, evaluated at k successes.
quantile(Binomial(n, q), p), the inverse of pbinom; p between 0 and 1. n trials with success probability q, evaluated at k successes.
A column of m random numbers, rand(rng, Binomial(n, q), m), drawn from Equavela's shared random generator (see Seed). n trials with success probability q, evaluated at k successes.
pdf(Cauchy(l, s), x). Location l, scale s > 0. All arguments are dimensionless real numbers; x may be an array (element by element).
cdf(Cauchy(l, s), x), the probability of a value up to x. Location l, scale s > 0.
quantile(Cauchy(l, s), p), the inverse of pcauchy; p between 0 and 1. Location l, scale s > 0.
A column of m random numbers, rand(rng, Cauchy(l, s), m), drawn from Equavela's shared random generator (see Seed). Location l, scale s > 0.
pdf(Chisq(d), x). d degrees of freedom; d need not be an integer. All arguments are dimensionless real numbers; x may be an array (element by element).
cdf(Chisq(d), x), the probability of a value up to x. d degrees of freedom; d need not be an integer.
quantile(Chisq(d), p), the inverse of pchisq; p between 0 and 1. d degrees of freedom; d need not be an integer.
A column of m random numbers, rand(rng, Chisq(d), m), drawn from Equavela's shared random generator (see Seed). d degrees of freedom; d need not be an integer.

pdf(Exponential(1/r), x). The parameter is the rate r, density r·e^(−r·x). Julia's Exponential(θ) takes the scale θ = 1/r. All arguments are dimensionless real numbers; x may be an array (element by element).
cdf(Exponential(1/r), x), the probability of a value up to x. The parameter is the rate r, density r·e^(−r·x). Julia's Exponential(θ) takes the scale θ = 1/r.
quantile(Exponential(1/r), p), the inverse of pexp; p between 0 and 1. The parameter is the rate r, density r·e^(−r·x). Julia's Exponential(θ) takes the scale θ = 1/r.

A column of m random numbers, rand(rng, Exponential(1/r), m), drawn from Equavela's shared random generator (see Seed). The parameter is the rate r, density r·e^(−r·x). Julia's Exponential(θ) takes the scale θ = 1/r.
pdf(FDist(d1, d2), x). d1, d2 degrees of freedom. All arguments are dimensionless real numbers; x may be an array (element by element).
cdf(FDist(d1, d2), x), the probability of a value up to x. d1, d2 degrees of freedom.
quantile(FDist(d1, d2), p), the inverse of pF; p between 0 and 1. d1, d2 degrees of freedom.
A column of m random numbers, rand(rng, FDist(d1, d2), m), drawn from Equavela's shared random generator (see Seed). d1, d2 degrees of freedom.

pdf(Gamma(s, 1), x). Shape s with unit scale; for another scale θ use dgamma(x/θ, s)/θ. Julia's Gamma(α, θ) also takes the scale. All arguments are dimensionless real numbers; x may be an array (element by element).
cdf(Gamma(s, 1), x), the probability of a value up to x. Shape s with unit scale; for another scale θ use dgamma(x/θ, s)/θ. Julia's Gamma(α, θ) also takes the scale.
quantile(Gamma(s, 1), p), the inverse of pgamma; p between 0 and 1. Shape s with unit scale; for another scale θ use dgamma(x/θ, s)/θ. Julia's Gamma(α, θ) also takes the scale.

A column of m random numbers, rand(rng, Gamma(s, 1), m), drawn from Equavela's shared random generator (see Seed). Shape s with unit scale; for another scale θ use dgamma(x/θ, s)/θ. Julia's Gamma(α, θ) also takes the scale.

pdf(Geometric(q), x). The number of failures before the first success, probability q·(1 − q)^k for k = 0, 1, …, as Julia's convention. For a non-integer argument the probability is 0. All arguments are dimensionless real numbers; x may be an array (element by element).

cdf(Geometric(q), x), the probability of a value up to x. The argument is rounded down to an integer first. The number of failures before the first success, probability q·(1 − q)^k for k = 0, 1, …, as Julia's convention.
quantile(Geometric(q), p), the inverse of pgeom; p between 0 and 1. The number of failures before the first success, probability q·(1 − q)^k for k = 0, 1, …, as Julia's convention.

A column of m random numbers, rand(rng, Geometric(q), m), drawn from Equavela's shared random generator (see Seed). The number of failures before the first success, probability q·(1 − q)^k for k = 0, 1, …, as Julia's convention.

pdf(Hypergeometric(a, b, n), x). m successes in n draws without replacement from a successes and b failures; Julia's Hypergeometric(s, f, n) with the same meaning. For a non-integer argument the probability is 0. All arguments are dimensionless real numbers; x may be an array (element by element).

cdf(Hypergeometric(a, b, n), x), the probability of a value up to x. The argument is rounded down to an integer first. m successes in n draws without replacement from a successes and b failures; Julia's Hypergeometric(s, f, n) with the same meaning.

quantile(Hypergeometric(a, b, n), p), the inverse of phypergeom; p between 0 and 1. m successes in n draws without replacement from a successes and b failures; Julia's Hypergeometric(s, f, n) with the same meaning.

A column of m random numbers, rand(rng, Hypergeometric(a, b, n), m), drawn from Equavela's shared random generator (see Seed). m successes in n draws without replacement from a successes and b failures; Julia's Hypergeometric(s, f, n) with the same meaning.
pdf(LogNormal(μ, σ), x). μ and σ are the mean and standard deviation of the logarithm, as Julia's LogNormal. All arguments are dimensionless real numbers; x may be an array (element by element).
cdf(LogNormal(μ, σ), x), the probability of a value up to x. μ and σ are the mean and standard deviation of the logarithm, as Julia's LogNormal.
quantile(LogNormal(μ, σ), p), the inverse of plnorm; p between 0 and 1. μ and σ are the mean and standard deviation of the logarithm, as Julia's LogNormal.

A column of m random numbers, rand(rng, LogNormal(μ, σ), m), drawn from Equavela's shared random generator (see Seed). μ and σ are the mean and standard deviation of the logarithm, as Julia's LogNormal.
pdf(Logistic(l, s), x). Location l, scale s > 0. All arguments are dimensionless real numbers; x may be an array (element by element).
cdf(Logistic(l, s), x), the probability of a value up to x. Location l, scale s > 0.
quantile(Logistic(l, s), p), the inverse of plogis; p between 0 and 1. Location l, scale s > 0.
A column of m random numbers, rand(rng, Logistic(l, s), m), drawn from Equavela's shared random generator (see Seed). Location l, scale s > 0.

pdf(NegativeBinomial(n, q), x). The number of failures k before the n-th success, with success probability q, as Julia's NegativeBinomial(r, p). For a non-integer argument the probability is 0. All arguments are dimensionless real numbers; x may be an array (element by element).

cdf(NegativeBinomial(n, q), x), the probability of a value up to x. The argument is rounded down to an integer first. The number of failures k before the n-th success, with success probability q, as Julia's NegativeBinomial(r, p).
quantile(NegativeBinomial(n, q), p), the inverse of pnbinom; p between 0 and 1. The number of failures k before the n-th success, with success probability q, as Julia's NegativeBinomial(r, p).

A column of m random numbers, rand(rng, NegativeBinomial(n, q), m), drawn from Equavela's shared random generator (see Seed). The number of failures k before the n-th success, with success probability q, as Julia's NegativeBinomial(r, p).
pdf(Normal(μ, σ), x). Mean μ, standard deviation σ > 0. All arguments are dimensionless real numbers; x may be an array (element by element).
cdf(Normal(μ, σ), x), the probability of a value up to x. Mean μ, standard deviation σ > 0.
quantile(Normal(μ, σ), p), the inverse of pnorm; p between 0 and 1. Mean μ, standard deviation σ > 0.
pdf(Poisson(λ), x). Mean λ > 0, evaluated at k events. For a non-integer argument the probability is 0. All arguments are dimensionless real numbers; x may be an array (element by element).
cdf(Poisson(λ), x), the probability of a value up to x. The argument is rounded down to an integer first. Mean λ > 0, evaluated at k events.
quantile(Poisson(λ), p), the inverse of ppois; p between 0 and 1. Mean λ > 0, evaluated at k events.
A column of m random numbers, rand(rng, Poisson(λ), m), drawn from Equavela's shared random generator (see Seed). Mean λ > 0, evaluated at k events.
pdf(TDist(d), x). d degrees of freedom; a non-central t is not provided. All arguments are dimensionless real numbers; x may be an array (element by element).
cdf(TDist(d), x), the probability of a value up to x. d degrees of freedom; a non-central t is not provided.
quantile(TDist(d), p), the inverse of pt; p between 0 and 1. d degrees of freedom; a non-central t is not provided.
A column of m random numbers, rand(rng, TDist(d), m), drawn from Equavela's shared random generator (see Seed). d degrees of freedom; a non-central t is not provided.
pdf(Uniform(a, b), x). Between a and b, with a < b. All arguments are dimensionless real numbers; x may be an array (element by element).
cdf(Uniform(a, b), x), the probability of a value up to x. Between a and b, with a < b.
quantile(Uniform(a, b), p), the inverse of punif; p between 0 and 1. Between a and b, with a < b.
A column of m random numbers, rand(rng, Uniform(a, b), m), drawn from Equavela's shared random generator (see Seed). Between a and b, with a < b.
pdf(Weibull(s, 1), x). Shape s with unit scale; Julia's Weibull(α, θ) also takes the scale. All arguments are dimensionless real numbers; x may be an array (element by element).
cdf(Weibull(s, 1), x), the probability of a value up to x. Shape s with unit scale; Julia's Weibull(α, θ) also takes the scale.
quantile(Weibull(s, 1), p), the inverse of pweibull; p between 0 and 1. Shape s with unit scale; Julia's Weibull(α, θ) also takes the scale.
A column of m random numbers, rand(rng, Weibull(s, 1), m), drawn from Equavela's shared random generator (see Seed). Shape s with unit scale; Julia's Weibull(α, θ) also takes the scale.
A column of m random numbers from the normal distribution with mean μ and standard deviation σ, from the shared random generator. Only the distribution is guaranteed, not particular values.
One uniformly distributed number in [0, x) from the shared generator: rand(rng)·x. Each evaluation gives a new number.

Resets the shared random generator, a Xoshiro generator owned by the calculation engine, to the seed x (an integer from 1 to 2147483647) and returns the previous seed. Without Seed, the generator is seeded from the clock when the engine starts, so random numbers differ from run to run; call Seed at the top of a worksheet for repeatable results.
The standard normal distribution function, cdf(Normal(), x); the same as pnorm(x, 0, 1).

The discrete Fourier transform Σ x[k]·e^(−2πi·jk/n) without normalisation, exactly fft(x). A matrix is transformed along both dimensions. The result keeps the shape of the input; units are kept. Element 0 of the result is the zero frequency.
The inverse of dft, dividing by the number of elements, as ifft.

The transform of real data: only the non-negative frequencies, n/2 + 1 values for n samples, as Julia's rfft. The length (or the number of columns of a matrix) must be even; imaginary parts are ignored.
The inverse of dftr: rebuilds the even-length real signal from the non-negative frequencies, as irfft(z, 2(length(z) − 1)).
An older transform convention: the positive exponent, scaled by 1/√n, that is ifft(x)·√n. Kept for older worksheets; use dft for new work.
The inverse of cfft: fft(x)/√n.

The local cosine packet table: a column of n + 1 vectors, levels 0 to n. Level l cuts the periodic signal into 2l blocks, folds it smoothly at the block boundaries and applies an orthonormal DCT-IV (FFTW.r2r(…, REDFT11)) to each block. The length must be a multiple of 2n+1; matrices are transformed along columns, then rows.
The analysis and synthesis filters of the spline wavelet of orders (m, n), as a two-column matrix. Only the pairs of the standard table are accepted.

The discrete wavelet transform with the four-coefficient Daubechies wavelet, as a pyramid down to two smooth coefficients. The length must be a power of two. Implemented directly; Julia's Wavelets.jl orders the coefficients differently.
The exact inverse of wave.

Evaluates at x the curve described by a vector made by cspline, lspline, pspline, bspline or loess for the same data: interp(cspline(vx, vy), vx, vy, x). Outside the data the end pieces continue (extrapolation). x may be an array. For two-dimensional data use the matrix form interp(vs, Mxy, Mz, X). Julia's Interpolations.jl works with interpolation objects instead of coefficient vectors.

The coefficient vector of an interpolating cubic spline whose ends are cubic (the second derivative is linear near the ends), for use with interp. The vector holds a header and the second derivatives at the data points. vx must ascend.
As cspline, with a natural end condition: the curve is straight at the ends (second derivative zero).
As cspline, with parabolic ends.
A B-spline of degree n that passes through the points, with the knots u (rows(vx) − n + 1 ascending values covering the data; the end knots are repeated). For use with interp.

A least-squares B-spline of degree n. Without knots, equally spaced knots are added until the Durbin–Watson statistic of the residuals reaches 2; with u, the given knots are used. vw gives the standard deviation of each point. The result is used by Binterp and DWS.
The value and the derivatives at x of the B-spline made by Spline2.
The Durbin–Watson statistic of the residuals of a Spline2 fit.
Interpolates the grid Z (Z[i, j] at (vx[i], vy[j])) at the point (p, q) with natural cubic splines, first along y, then along x; it extrapolates linearly outside.
Linear interpolation of the points (vx, vy) at x; outside the data the end segments are extended. vx must ascend. x may be an array.
n values that continue the evenly spaced data v, by Burg's (maximum entropy) linear prediction with m coefficients.
Polynomial interpolation through all points by Neville's algorithm, starting at the point nearest to x: the vector [value; error], the error being the signed last correction.
The coefficients, constant term first, of the polynomial of degree n − 1 through the n points. The inverse of evaluating a polynomial; compare Polynomials.fit in Julia.
The column [converged; order; value]: Neville's interpolation of increasing order up to N, stopping when the correction is at most e times the value.
Rational function interpolation (Bulirsch–Stoer) at x: [value; error]. A pole is an error.
The coefficients of Thiele's continued fraction through the points, for Thiele.
Evaluates Thiele's continued fraction a₀ + (x − x₀)/(a₁ + (x − x₁)/(a₂ + …)) at x.

All roots of the polynomial with the coefficients v, constant term first (2 to 99 coefficients, the last non-zero), as the eigenvalues of the companion matrix. Real roots come back as real numbers. Equivalent to Polynomials.roots(Polynomial(v)) in Julia.
Local quadratic regression with tricube weights over the nearest span·N points, for use with interp. Works with one variable (vectors) or several (a matrix of points).
The least-squares line as [intercept; slope].
The slope of the least-squares line.
The intercept of the least-squares line.
The standard error of the linear regression, √(Σresiduals²/(n − 2)).
Tukey's resistant median–median line, [intercept; slope].
Fits (a₀ + … + aₘxᵐ)/(1 + b₁x + … + bₙxⁿ) by Levenberg–Marquardt; each row is a parameter [value, lower, upper] with conf confidence limits (rows a₀…aₘ, then b₁…bₙ).
As rationalfit, penalising a denominator that approaches zero inside the data range, so the fit has no poles there.

Multivariate polynomial regression. The third argument is the degree (all terms up to that total degree), a string naming the terms ("A,AA": A the first variable, AA its square, AB the product with the second), or a matrix of exponents. The result is a function of one argument: a number for one variable, a vector of the variables otherwise.
The coefficient table of polyfit: a header row and one row per term with coefficient, standard error, confidence limits, variance inflation factor, t value and one-sided p value.

The statistics of polyfit: standard deviation, R², adjusted and predicted R², PRESS, Durbin–Watson, the coefficient table, the ANOVA table and per-observation diagnostics (leverage, studentised residuals, Cook's distance, DFFITS).

Fits the parameters u of a function F(x, u) by Levenberg–Marquardt, starting at vg. F may return the value followed by its partial derivatives; otherwise they are computed numerically. Compare LsqFit.curve_fit in Julia.
The coefficients [A; b; C] of A·e^(b·x) + C; the guess vg is optional.
The coefficients [a; b] of a·ln(x) + b (a linear fit in ln x).
The coefficients of a·ln(x + b) + c.
The coefficients of the logistic curve a/(1 + b·e^(−c·x)).
The coefficients of a·x^b + c.
The coefficients of a·sin(x + b) + c.

Fits the scalar function F(x, u) and returns, per parameter, [value, lower, upper] with conf confidence limits. Optional: the standard deviations of y (a vector), bounds (a two-column matrix) and the accuracy (a scalar), recognised by their shape.
For fitted parameters b of F(x, u): the half-width of the conf confidence interval of each parameter (first column) and the Student t value used.
The least-squares coefficients of a linear combination of the basis functions returned (as a column) by F(x). Julia equivalent: build the design matrix and solve with \.
As genfit for several independent variables: the rows of X are passed to F as column vectors.

The number of data values in each interval; intervals include their left end, and the last one both ends. intvls is either a vector of ascending interval boundaries (one fewer result than boundaries) or a number of equal intervals spanning the data. Compare StatsBase.fit(Histogram, data, edges).
A two-column matrix for plotting: the midpoints of the intervals and the frequencies, with the intervals given as for hist.
For each column of Data, the values that draw a box plot: minimum, quartiles, median and maximum.
Two vectors that draw a box plot as XY traces in an ordinary plot.
From a two-column matrix of names and positive values: the rows sorted by decreasing value, with a third column holding the cumulative percentage, for a Pareto chart.

The full factorial design of k factors with 2 levels (or levels levels), first factor changing fastest (Yates order). A design matrix has a header row ("Run", "Block", then the factor names A, B, …) and one row per run with the coded levels (−1/+1, or 0, 1, 2 for three levels).
The two-level fractional factorial design 2k−p: the first k − p factors in Yates order and p generated factors (named with their generator, for example "D=ABC") from the standard generator table.
The Plackett–Burman screening design of n runs (a multiple of 4 from 8 to 48) for n − 1 factors.
The Box–Behnken response-surface design for 3 to 7 factors, with its blocks and centre runs.
The Taguchi orthogonal array for k factors at the given number of levels (L4, L8, L9, L12, L27 …); other combinations are an error.
The runs of a design matrix in a random order; run numbers move with their rows. Uses the shared random generator (see Seed).
The design followed by its fold-over block with every sign reversed, or only the named factor (a string such as "A") reversed.
Replaces the coded levels of a design matrix with real values: L has a row per factor with its name and one value per level.
The effect of each factor at each level (mean response at that level minus the grand mean). A number k adds the interactions up to order k; a string such as "AB" selects one term.
For a −1/+1 design: the mean response at the low and the high level of each term and their difference.
The analysis of variance of a replicated design (the columns of Y are the replicates): source, sum of squares, degrees of freedom, mean square, F and p.
n draws of the standard normal distribution, as a column; intended as the distribution argument of montecarlo.
n draws uniformly distributed on [−6, 6], so that mean + σ·r spans six standard deviations; for montecarlo.
n draws of the lognormal distribution with parameters 0 and 1; for montecarlo.
n draws of the Weibull distribution of shape 1 and scale 1; for montecarlo.

n samples of the function F at random arguments. Rvals has a row per argument of F: its name, mean and standard deviation; each argument is mean + σ·r with r drawn from dist (Normal by default, or a function of your own). Limits (lower and upper, NaN for none) truncates a variable: a value outside is drawn again.
The triangular window of n points, rising from 0 to 1 and back to 0.
The symmetric Hamming window 0.54 − 0.46·cos(2πk/(n − 1)) of n points. Same values as DSP.hamming(n).
The symmetric Hann window 0.5 − 0.5·cos(2πk/(n − 1)) of n points (DSP.hanning).
The symmetric Blackman window 0.42 − 0.5·cos(2πk/(n−1)) + 0.08·cos(4πk/(n−1)) (DSP.blackman).
The Gaussian window exp(−½·(a·k/((n − 1)/2))²) for k from −(n − 1)/2 to (n − 1)/2.
The two columns of a quantile–quantile plot: the sorted data against the matching quantiles of a second data set or of a named distribution (the normal distribution by default).
Grubbs's test for outliers at significance a, applied repeatedly: the indices of the suspected outliers, their test statistics and their distances to the critical value.
The classic single-outlier Grubbs test: the most likely outlier, if any.
The indices of the points more than three standard deviations from the mean.
The vector or matrix without the elements (or rows) at the indices vindex, counted from ORIGIN. Julia equivalent: deleteat! on a copy.
A copy of M with the indexed elements set to NaN.
The indices of the NaN elements.
M without the rows that contain NaN. Julia equivalent: M[.!any(isnan, M, dims=2)[:], :].

Principal component analysis of the columns of DATA by the NIPALS algorithm, extracting NumPC components with at most maxiter iterations each, on scaled or unscaled data. The result feeds scores, loadings, PCAeigenvals, PCAvariance and Nipals2. Components agree with an eigen-decomposition up to sign.
Extends a Nipals result with more components.
The score matrix of a Nipals result.
The loading matrix of a Nipals result.
The eigenvalues of the principal components of a Nipals result.
The cumulative percentage of variance explained by the principal components.
The positions and values of local maxima: of a matrix of heights (M1), or of Z over the grid x, y; w is the half-width of the neighbourhood examined.
As localmax, for minima.
Friedman's super smoother: running-line smoothers with spans of 5, 20 and 50 % of the data, choosing the span point by point by cross-validation.
A normalised Gaussian kernel smoother; the standard deviation of the kernel is the bandwidth b, in the units of vx.
A centred running median with an odd window n (3 by default); at the ends of a vector the window shrinks. For a matrix, n × m windows.
A repeated running median: for each window width of w, the median smoother is applied until the result stops changing (within TOL).
Exponential smoothing sᵢ = a·vᵢ + (1 − a)·sᵢ₋₁, starting at the first value; 0 ≤ a ≤ 1.
The trailing moving average over n values; the first values average over the elements available so far.

The classical fourth-order Runge–Kutta method with intvls equal steps. The table solvers return a matrix with intvls + 1 rows: the points in the first column, then one column per unknown. D(x, y) receives the unknowns as a column vector and returns their derivatives; init holds the initial values (a scalar for one equation). x2 < x1 integrates backwards. Implemented in Equavela's runtime; Julia users would reach for DifferentialEquations.jl, whose solvers return solution objects rather than tables.

Runge–Kutta with adaptive steps (Dormand–Prince 5(4) pair), reporting at intvls equally spaced points. The internal tolerance is tighter than TOL. The table solvers return a matrix with intvls + 1 rows: the points in the first column, then one column per unknown. D(x, y) receives the unknowns as a column vector and returns their derivatives; init holds the initial values (a scalar for one equation). x2 < x1 integrates backwards. Implemented in Equavela's runtime; Julia users would reach for DifferentialEquations.jl, whose solvers return solution objects rather than tables.

Gragg–Bulirsch–Stoer extrapolation, efficient for smooth problems. The table solvers return a matrix with intvls + 1 rows: the points in the first column, then one column per unknown. D(x, y) receives the unknowns as a column vector and returns their derivatives; init holds the initial values (a scalar for one equation). x2 < x1 integrates backwards. Implemented in Equavela's runtime; Julia users would reach for DifferentialEquations.jl, whose solvers return solution objects rather than tables.

The fourth-order Adams–Bashforth–Moulton predictor-corrector for non-stiff problems, refining the internal steps until two runs agree within tol. The table solvers return a matrix with intvls + 1 rows: the points in the first column, then one column per unknown. D(x, y) receives the unknowns as a column vector and returns their derivatives; init holds the initial values (a scalar for one equation). x2 < x1 integrates backwards. Implemented in Equavela's runtime; Julia users would reach for DifferentialEquations.jl, whose solvers return solution objects rather than tables.

The backward differentiation formula with Newton iterations, for stiff problems; J(x, y) is the Jacobian (computed numerically when omitted). The table solvers return a matrix with intvls + 1 rows: the points in the first column, then one column per unknown. D(x, y) receives the unknowns as a column vector and returns their derivatives; init holds the initial values (a scalar for one equation). x2 < x1 integrates backwards. Implemented in Equavela's runtime; Julia users would reach for DifferentialEquations.jl, whose solvers return solution objects rather than tables.

Radau IIA (order 5), for stiff problems and differential-algebraic systems: the optional mass matrix M solves M·y′ = D(x, y). The table solvers return a matrix with intvls + 1 rows: the points in the first column, then one column per unknown. D(x, y) receives the unknowns as a column vector and returns their derivatives; init holds the initial values (a scalar for one equation). x2 < x1 integrates backwards. Implemented in Equavela's runtime; Julia users would reach for DifferentialEquations.jl, whose solvers return solution objects rather than tables.

Linearly implicit Euler extrapolation for stiff systems; AJ(x, y) returns the augmented Jacobian [∂D/∂x, ∂D/∂y]. The table solvers return a matrix with intvls + 1 rows: the points in the first column, then one column per unknown. D(x, y) receives the unknowns as a column vector and returns their derivatives; init holds the initial values (a scalar for one equation). x2 < x1 integrates backwards. Implemented in Equavela's runtime; Julia users would reach for DifferentialEquations.jl, whose solvers return solution objects rather than tables.

A Rosenbrock method for stiff systems; AJ as for Stiffb. The table solvers return a matrix with intvls + 1 rows: the points in the first column, then one column per unknown. D(x, y) receives the unknowns as a column vector and returns their derivatives; init holds the initial values (a scalar for one equation). x2 < x1 integrates backwards. Implemented in Equavela's runtime; Julia users would reach for DifferentialEquations.jl, whose solvers return solution objects rather than tables.

Chooses BDF when the problem looks stiff at the start (the spectral radius of the Jacobian times the output step exceeds 1) and Adams otherwise. The table solvers return a matrix with intvls + 1 rows: the points in the first column, then one column per unknown. D(x, y) receives the unknowns as a column vector and returns their derivatives; init holds the initial values (a scalar for one equation). x2 < x1 integrates backwards. Implemented in Equavela's runtime; Julia users would reach for DifferentialEquations.jl, whose solvers return solution objects rather than tables.

Solves the linear system x′ = A(t)·x + B(t)·u(t); A, B and u may be functions of t or constant arrays. The table solvers return a matrix with intvls + 1 rows: the points in the first column, then one column per unknown. D(x, y) receives the unknowns as a column vector and returns their derivatives; init holds the initial values (a scalar for one equation). x2 < x1 integrates backwards. Implemented in Equavela's runtime; Julia users would reach for DifferentialEquations.jl, whose solvers return solution objects rather than tables.

For a boundary value problem: the initial values missing at x1, found by shooting (adaptive Runge–Kutta and Levenberg–Marquardt). load1(x1, v1) builds the initial vector from the guesses and score(x2, y) measures the mismatch at the far end.
As sbval, shooting from both ends to the match point xf: the row of values missing at x1 followed by those missing at x2.

The method of lines for one-dimensional time-dependent partial differential equations: space is discretised on xpts points with fourth-order differences, time integrated with Radau. bc_func gives, per equation, the left and right boundary values and their type ("D" Dirichlet, "N" Neumann). The result has xpts rows and, for each function, tpts columns.

Solves the five-point finite-difference equation A·u[i+1,j] + B·u[i−1,j] + C·u[i,j+1] + D·u[i,j−1] + E·u[i,j] = S[i,j] (Poisson or Laplace on a grid) by red–black successive over-relaxation with Chebyshev acceleration; U holds the boundary values and the starting guess, rjac the spectral radius of the Jacobi iteration.
Solves Poisson's equation ∇²u = M on the unit square with zero boundary by the multigrid method with ncycle V-cycles per level; M must be square with 2k + 1 rows.

Used as the closing call of a solve block of differential equations (see Solving equations): the solution as a function of the independent variable, between the first condition point and b. Initial value problems are integrated with an adaptive Adams/BDF scheme; conditions at two points are met by shooting.

A general reader. "type" is "delimited", "fixed" (then colwidths gives the column widths), "Excel" (.xls and .xlsx) or an OpenDocument spreadsheet. rows and cols select a block, emptyfill replaces missing values (NaN by default), decsymb sets the decimal symbol. Numbers become numbers and other cells strings. A relative file name is relative to the worksheet's folder (CWD).
Writes a matrix to a spreadsheet (.ods, .xls, .xlsx) or, for other extensions, to tab-delimited text. A relative file name is relative to the worksheet's folder (CWD).

Reads delimited or fixed-width text with options for the delimiter, column widths, the rows and columns to read ("rowspec", "colspec"), the value of empty cells and how blank rows are treated. A relative file name is relative to the worksheet's folder (CWD).
Writes a matrix as tab-delimited text, optionally only the given rows and columns, with the chosen decimal symbol. A relative file name is relative to the worksheet's folder (CWD).

Reads raw binary data of the given "type" ("byte", "uint16", "int32", "float", "double" …) and byte order (0 little-endian, 1 big-endian) into a matrix with cols columns, skipping skip bytes. Julia equivalent: read! into an array plus ltoh/ntoh. A relative file name is relative to the worksheet's folder (CWD).
Writes a matrix as raw binary data of the given type and byte order. A relative file name is relative to the worksheet's folder (CWD).
Reads a comma-separated file into a matrix; numeric cells become numbers, others strings. A relative file name is relative to the worksheet's folder (CWD).
Writes a matrix as comma-separated values, optionally only the given rows and columns, with the chosen decimal symbol. A relative file name is relative to the worksheet's folder (CWD).

Reads a structured data file: whitespace-separated numeric rows, or the block format that WRITEPRN uses for complex, string and nested matrices. A relative file name is relative to the worksheet's folder (CWD).

Writes a matrix as structured data: real numbers as rows with PRNCOLWIDTH columns of width and PRNPRECISION significant digits; complex, string or nested matrices in a block format that READPRN reads back. Returns the matrix written. A relative file name is relative to the worksheet's folder (CWD).

Appends the rows of M to a structured data file (the columns must match) and returns M. Writes are serialised, so a loop can log results safely. A relative file name is relative to the worksheet's folder (CWD).

Writes a matrix into an .xlsx or .xls workbook, optionally into a range such as "Sheet1!B2". An existing .xls with features that cannot be preserved safely is refused rather than damaged. A relative file name is relative to the worksheet's folder (CWD).

Reads an image (BMP, GIF, JPEG, TGA, PCX, PBM, PGM, PPM, TIFF, PNG) as a matrix of grey levels from 0 to 255, one element per pixel, rows from the top. A relative file name is relative to the worksheet's folder (CWD).
As READ_IMAGE, for bitmap files.
Writes a matrix of grey levels (0 to 255) as a greyscale bitmap. A relative file name is relative to the worksheet's folder (CWD).
Reads a colour image as one matrix with the red, green and blue planes side by side (three times as many columns as pixels).
Writes a colour image from a matrix with the red, green and blue planes side by side.
The red plane of a colour image, 0 to 255.
The green plane.
The blue plane.
The hue, lightness and saturation planes side by side, each scaled to 0–255.
Writes a colour image from hue, lightness and saturation planes side by side.
The hue, saturation and value planes side by side, each scaled to 0–255.
Writes a colour image from hue, saturation and value planes.
The saturation plane of the HLS model.
The saturation plane of the HSV model.
The lightness plane.
The value plane.
The hue plane (the same in the HLS and HSV models).
The samples of a WAV file as a matrix, one column per channel, as integers in the range of the file's resolution. A relative file name is relative to the worksheet's folder (CWD).
Writes the columns of M as the channels of a WAV file with sample rate s (Hz) and resolution b (bits). A relative file name is relative to the worksheet's folder (CWD).
A vector with the number of channels, the sample rate, the resolution and the average bytes per second.

Reads a range of an OpenDocument spreadsheet (.ods, the LibreOffice Calc format, which Excel also reads and writes) as a matrix. The range is "B2", "A1:C10", "Sheet name!A1:C10" (or with a period) or "'My sheet'!A1:B2"; without one, the used range of the first sheet. Numbers become numbers, text strings; empty cells take emptyfill (NaN by default). Implemented in Equavela's runtime, with no spreadsheet application needed. A relative file name is relative to the worksheet's folder (CWD).

Writes a matrix into the named sheet of an OpenDocument workbook (the first sheet by default), creating the file if needed and keeping the other sheets and their content. A relative file name is relative to the worksheet's folder (CWD).

Without an interval, the secant method from the guess (the current value of x; a complex guess finds complex roots), accepting the point only if |f(x)| ≤ TOL. With an interval [a, b] where f changes sign, bisection to machine precision. Units are allowed: the result has the unit of the guess or of the bounds. The first argument is an expression of the variable, not a function value, so root(x² − 2, x) works directly. Compare Roots.find_zero in Julia. A worksheet definition named root takes precedence; the n-th root is the operator ⁿ√x.

Levenberg–Marquardt on the residuals of the equations and the violations of the inequalities, starting from the guess values; succeeds only when every constraint holds within CTOL. With one unknown it returns its value, with several a column vector in call order. find(x, y) → solves symbolically. May be written Find.
The same algorithm as find, returning the best point found even when the constraints are not met; check the result.

A quadratic penalty method (weights 10, 10³, 10⁵, 10⁷), each stage minimised by BFGS with central-difference gradients. f is named without arguments. The final point must satisfy the constraints within CTOL. Compare Optim.optimize in Julia.
As minimize, for the largest value.
